summary: Updates the URN namespace for National Bibliography Numbers, identifiers national libraries use for resources not covered by standard identifier systems such as ISBN. It revises the namespace that was established in 2001.

plainLanguage.summary: Each national library numbers the things it looks after, and those numbers are useful locally but mean nothing elsewhere. This RFC explains how to write such a number as a URN, a permanent name of the form urn:nbn followed by the country code and the library's own number. The country code makes the name unique worldwide, and the rules make sure that once a name has been given out it is never given to something else.

questions: what is a national bibliography number
how is a urn nbn resolved
what does urn nbn syntax look like
subtitle: How national libraries turn their own local identifiers into permanent names on the Internet.

tldr.problem: A national library keeps its own local identifier for everything it holds, including the many things that have no ISBN or ISSN. Those identifiers are unique inside the country but say nothing to the rest of the world, and they do not survive a change of format.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how such an identifier is written as a URN: a country code, optional sub-namespace codes, a hyphen and the local identifier, with rules on case, on persistence and on how the name is resolved.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that replaces RFC 3188 with a registration in the current IANA template. URN:NBNs are already in production use in nine European countries.

facts.label: Prefix
facts.value: The ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code of the library's country, plus optional sub-namespace codes

facts.label: Delimiting character
facts.value: A hyphen between the prefix and the NBN string

facts.label: Countries in production use
facts.value: Austria, Finland, Germany, Hungary, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and Switzerland

today: RFC 8458 was published in October 2018 as an Informational document and replaces RFC 3188, whose namespace registration it brings up to date. It has not been obsoleted or updated since. The document records that URN:NBNs are in production use in nine European countries and that tens of millions have been assigned since 2001.

sections.title: What a National Bibliography Number Is
sections.content:
One of the basic permanent Uniform Resource Identifier schemes is Uniform Resource Name, originally defined in RFC 2141 and revised in 2017 with new definitions and registration procedures. Any traditional identifier, when used within the URN system, must have a namespace of its own that is registered with IANA. National Bibliography Number is one such namespace, specified in 2001 in RFC 3188.

This document describes the syntax and usage of NBN URNs and updates the registration of the associated URN namespace. It also describes certain policy assumptions about how national libraries and their partner organizations partition, delegate and manage the namespace, and notes that violation of those assumptions could affect the utility of the namespace.

The term National Bibliography Number encompasses persistent local identifier systems that national libraries and their partner organizations use in addition to the more formally established identifiers. These partner organizations include universities and their libraries, other research institutions, and governmental and public organizations. Some national libraries maintain a significant number of these relationships: the German National Library had almost 400 by early 2018.

In practice, NBN differs from standard identifier systems such as ISBN and ISSN because it is not a single identifier system with a standard-specified scope and syntax. Each NBN implementer creates its own system with its own syntax and assignment rules, each user organization is obliged to keep track of how NBNs are being used, and within the generic framework set in this document, local assignment policies may vary considerably. Historically, NBNs were applied to identify the resources catalogued into the national bibliographies, and before the bibliographic standard identifiers of the early 1970s, national libraries assigned NBNs to all catalogued publications. Since the late 1990s the scope has extended to a vast range of resources, both originally digital and digitized, and only a small subset of these is catalogued in the national bibliographies. Digitized resources and their component parts, such as still images in books or journal articles, are examples that may get NBNs. The scope can be extended further still: the National Library of Finland uses NBNs in its Finnish National Ontology Service to identify corporate names, which provides a stable basis for linked data.
sections.plainLanguage: Every library numbers its own stock, and those numbers are not governed by any international rule, so each library makes its own. This document is the common frame around all of them: it says how to write one of these numbers so that it means the same thing everywhere, without dictating how any individual library should number its own holdings.

sections.title: The Namespace and Who Runs It
sections.content:
NBNs are widely used to identify both hand-held and digital resources in the collections of national libraries and other institutions responsible for preserving the cultural heritage of their constituents. Resources in these collections are usually preserved for a long time, for centuries. The preferred method for digital preservation has traditionally been migration, whereby a resource in an outdated file format is moved into a more modern one, and to the extent possible all old versions are also kept, to soften the effects of partially successful migrations and the gradual loss of original look and feel. When NBN is used to identify manifestations and there are many of them for a single work, local policy can require that each manifestation have its own NBN.

NBNs are typically used for objects for which standard identifiers such as ISBN are not applicable, but they can be used for component resources even when the resource as a whole qualifies for a standard identifier. If a digitized book has an ISBN, the JPEG image files of its pages might be assigned NBNs, and those URNs can be used as persistent links to the pages. One of the roles of the NBN is to fill in the gaps left by the standard identifiers, so that together they cover all the resources national libraries and their partners need to include in their collections.

National libraries are the key organizations providing persistent URN resolution services, and as coordinators of NBN usage they have allowed other organizations, such as university libraries or governmental organizations, to assign NBNs to the resources those organizations preserve for the long term. URN:NBNs are expected to be resolvable and to support one or more resolution services. Resources identified by NBNs are not always available on the Internet, and if one is not, the URN can resolve to a surrogate such as a metadata record describing the identified resource.

There are at least two ways of taking component resources into account. The simplest and probably most common is to assign a separate NBN for each component resource and make no provisions to make such NBNs discernible in a systematic way from others. The second is to attach the f-component to a URN:NBN, if the stipulations of the URI generic syntax and the media type specification are met, to indicate the desired location within the resource supplied by resolution. From the library community point of view it is important that the f-component is not part of the namespace-specific string, so attaching it does not mean the component part is identified, and the resolution process still retrieves the entire resource even if there is an f-component: the component part selection is applied by the resolution client. In the first case the component parts are independently named entities, and in the second they are logical and physical parts of the identified resource.
sections.plainLanguage: Libraries keep things for centuries, so the names they use have to last, and they need a way to point at part of a thing as well as at the whole. A part can be named in two ways: give it its own number, or attach a location to the number of the whole. The second way is only a pointer for the reader's software to act on; the resolution still hands back the entire resource.

sections.title: The Syntax of an NBN URN
sections.content:
Assignment of NBN-based URNs is controlled on a national level by the national library, or by the national libraries if there is more than one. National guidelines can differ, but the identified resources themselves are usually persistent. Each national library uses NBNs independently of other national libraries, and apart from this document there are no guidelines that specify or control NBN usage, so NBNs are unique only on the national level. When used as URNs, base NBN strings must be augmented with a controlled prefix, which is the particular nation's ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 two-letter country code. These prefixes guarantee the uniqueness of the URNs at global scale. Once an NBN has been assigned to a resource it must be persistent, and therefore URNs are persistent as well. A URN, once generated from an NBN, must not be reused for another resource, and users must ensure they do not assign the same URN twice. Different policies can be applied to guarantee this, for instance by assigning NBNs sequentially by program, or by using printable representations of checksums such as SHA-1 as NBNs.

The namespace-specific string consists of three parts: a prefix consisting of an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code and optional sub-namespace codes separated by colons; a hyphen as the delimiting character; and the NBN string assigned by the national library or a sub-delegated authority. The structure of the NBN string is determined by the authority for the prefix. The prefix is regarded as case insensitive, but NBN strings can be case sensitive at the preference of the assigning authority, so parsers must treat them as case sensitive and any case mapping needed to introduce case insensitivity is the responsibility of the relevant resolution system.

A colon should be used within the prefix only as a delimiting character between the country code and the sub-namespace codes, which splits the national namespace into smaller parts. A hyphen should be used as the delimiting character between the prefix and the NBN string, and within the NBN string a hyphen may be used to separate sections of the identifier. All two-letter codes are reserved by the ISO 3166 Maintenance Agency for either existing or possible future country codes, or for private use. Sub-namespace identifiers must be registered on the national level by the national library that assigned the identifier, and the list can be made publicly available over the Web. Being part of the prefix, sub-namespace identifier strings are case insensitive, and they must not contain any colons or hyphens.

Two URNs are lexically equivalent if they are octet-by-octet equal after converting all characters in the leading urn:nbn: token to a single case, converting all characters in the prefix to a single case, and converting all characters embedded in any percent-encodings to a single case. Resolvers do not currently support the use of either the r-component or the q-component. The f-component may be used to indicate a location within the identified resource when the media type supports it, and persistence is achieved if the URN is assigned to one and only one version of a resource.
sections.plainLanguage: The name has three pieces: a country code, optionally followed by colon-separated sub-namespace codes that the library itself hands out, then a hyphen, then the library's own number. The country code is what makes the name unique worldwide, and the rule that a name is never reused is what makes it a permanent name rather than a temporary label.

sections.title: Resolving and Staying Persistent
sections.content:
Eventually, URNs might be resolved with the help of a Global Resolver Discovery Service, and the URN:NBN syntax makes it possible to locate the relevant resolver. Since no such system has been installed in the Internet, URN:NBNs are embedded in HTTP URIs in order to make them actionable in the present Internet, and in these HTTP URIs the authority part must point to the appropriate URN resolution service. In Finland, the address of the national URN resolver is urn.fi, so the HTTP URI for the Finnish URN in the example is http://urn.fi/URN:NBN:fi-fe201003181510. The country-code-based prefix part of the namespace-specific string will provide the hint needed to find the correct resolution service once a global discovery service exists.

There are three interrelated aspects of persistence. Persistence of the object itself, persistence of the identifier, and persistence of the URN resolvers. NBNs have traditionally been assigned to printed resources, which tend to be persistent, whereas digital resources require frequent migrations to guarantee accessibility. Although it is impossible to estimate how often migrations are needed, hardware and software upgrades take place frequently, and a lifetime exceeding 10 to 20 years can be considered as long.

It is common practice to keep the original and previously migrated versions as well, so even outdated versions remain available in digital archives no matter how old or difficult to use they have become. If all versions are kept, a user who requires authenticity can retrieve the original version, while a user for whom ease of use is the priority will be satisfied with the latest version. To enable users to find the best match, a national library can link all manifestations of a resource to each other. Thus, even if specific versions of digital resources are not normally persistent, persistent identifiers support information architectures that enable persistent access to any version, including ones that can only be used with digital archaeology tools such as custom-made applications to render the resource. Persistence of the URN resolvers themselves is mainly an organizational issue related to the persistence of the organizations maintaining them, and since resolution services will be supplied primarily by national libraries, these services are likely to be long lived.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no global directory of names yet, so a NBN is put inside a web address that points at the country's own resolver. Keeping a name working takes three things to last: the thing itself, the number given to it, and the service that looks it up. The library keeps old versions rather than overwriting them, so a name can still lead to the original file even after the format has moved on.

sections.title: The URN Namespace Registration
sections.content:
The URN namespace registration describes how National Bibliography Numbers can be supported within the URN framework, and it uses the updated IANA template specified in RFC 8141. The namespace identifier is NBN. This namespace ID was formally assigned in October 2001, when the namespace was registered officially, although utilization of URN:NBNs had started in demo systems already in 1998. Since 2001, tens of millions of URN:NBNs have been assigned, and the number of users has grown in two ways: new national libraries have started using NBNs, and many national libraries using the system have formed new liaisons. The registration version is 4, dated 2018-04-09.

The registrant is Juha Hakala, Senior Adviser at the National Library of Finland, who registered the namespace on behalf of the Conference of European National Librarians and the Conference of Directors of National Libraries. The NBN namespace is available for free to the national libraries, which can allow other organizations to assign URNs and use the resolution services established by the library, free of charge or for a fee, and the fees, if collected, can be based on the maintenance costs of the system.

The revision information records what changed. This version of the registration has been updated to use the revised definition of URN syntax from RFC 8141, although usage of r-components is not specified yet. Non-ISO 3166 country-code based NBNs have been deleted due to lack of deployment. The entire NBN prefix is now specified to be case insensitive, in accordance with established practice. The version also includes numerous clarifications based on actual usage of URNs.
sections.plainLanguage: The central registry of URN namespaces holds the entry for NBN, now at version 4. The entry records who runs it, which is the National Library of Finland acting for the European national libraries, and it notes that the namespace is free for national libraries to use. The changes in this version are mostly tidying up after seventeen years of real use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document defines means of encoding NBNs as URNs, and it depicts a URN resolution service for NBN-based URNs only at a generic level, so questions of secure or authenticated resolution mechanisms and of authenticating users are out of scope.

Although no validation mechanisms are specified on the global level, beyond a routine check of those characters that require special encoding when employed in URIs, NBNs assigned by any given authority can have a well-specified and rich syntax, including a fixed length and a checksum, and in such cases it is possible to validate the correctness of NBNs programmatically.

Issues regarding intellectual property rights associated with objects identified by the URNs are beyond the scope of this document, as are questions about rights to the databases that might be used to construct resolution services. Beyond the general security considerations of the underlying documents, no specific security threats have been identified for NBN-based URNs.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC leaves the security of the lookup service itself alone, because it only describes how the name is written. What it does note is that a library whose own numbering scheme includes a check digit can have that checked automatically, which catches typos and mistakes in the number before anyone acts on it.

nbn-nss     = prefix "-" nbn-string

prefix      = iso-cc *( ":" subspc )
iso-cc      = 2ALPHA
subspc      = 1*(ALPHA / DIGIT)
nbn-string  = path-rootless
